Upload a GeoJSON, find out which geometries are invalid and why, and
run the same diagnosis in Python and in R on the same map. Repair
(`make_valid()`/`st_make_valid()`) is a separate, optional step, at
the bottom of the page.

A `.geojson`, or a shapefile (either as a single `.zip`, or as
`.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` selected together): see the section below.

Just want to quickly validate or fix a file, without the rest of the
reading? Use the
[standalone tool](/tools/geojson-shapefile-validator.html) — same
engine, less prose.

::: {#lab-upload}
:::

## Can a polygon look normal and still be invalid?

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["🗺️ Looks fine on the map"] --> B{"Validity check"}
    B --> C["❌ INVALID: why?"]
```

Yes: a polygon can have a boundary that crosses itself, a hole that
extends outside the outer boundary, or two holes that overlap, and it's
not uncommon for the shape on the map to look perfectly fine. Below you
can find out exactly what to look for, in your own file or in one of
the six ready-made examples further down.

## Shared map and table

A single map and table, shared by every example on the page: run the
same diagnosis in Python or R and compare the result here. The two
languages draw to two separate layers: running one doesn't clear or
change what the other already drew, so both stay visible together
(and in their own tab in the table below) for a direct comparison.
Running R doesn't "correct" or replace Python's result, and vice
versa. If you want to see a language's result change, re-run that
language's own cell.

## Diagnose: validate your geometry

Run the same check in Python or R on the current data: your file
uploaded above, or, if you haven't uploaded one, the bowtie example
below (the diagnosis cells load it automatically when there's no
upload). No repair yet, just diagnosis: is the geometry valid? If
not, why?

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #geometry-diagnose-py}
#| package: geopandas, shapely
import re
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import shape
from shapely.validation import explain_validity

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

if gdf is None:
    bowtie = {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[12.45, 41.85], [12.55, 41.95], [12.45, 41.95], [12.55, 41.85], [12.45, 41.85]]]}
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": ["bowtie"]}, geometry=[shape(bowtie)], crs="EPSG:4326")

# Diagnosis and the map both need WGS84 (GeoJSON/MapLibre assume it) —
# original_crs/export_crs stay in the session as globals, reused by
# geometry-repair-py below to reproject BACK before a download.
crs_warning = None
original_crs = gdf.crs
if original_crs is None:
    gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
    original_crs = gdf.crs
    crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
elif original_crs != "EPSG:4326":
    gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

def export_crs(g):
    if g is None or original_crs is None or original_crs == "EPSG:4326":
        return g
    return g.to_crs(original_crs)

if "name" not in gdf.columns:
    gdf["name"] = [f"geometry {i+1}" for i in range(len(gdf))]

# explain_validity() sometimes appends the failure coordinates in
# brackets (e.g. "Self-intersection[12.5 41.9]") — split that into its
# own "position" column instead of leaving it inside the message.
POSITION_RE = re.compile(r"^(.*?)\[([-\d.]+)\s+([-\d.]+)\]$")

# GEOS reports one of a small, CLOSED set of validity failures --
# verified against TopologyValidationError.cpp in the GEOS source
# itself (see "Gallery of geometric errors" below), not guessed from
# whichever examples this article happens to show. The raw message
# always starts with one of these exact names before any bracketed
# position, so "category" is that name itself; with the position split
# off, the rest of the message never says anything more, which is why
# there's no separate "reason" column here (R's own, below, does say
# something different).
GEOS_CATEGORIES = [
    "Ring Self-intersection",
    "Self-intersection",
    "Hole lies outside shell",
    "Holes are nested",
    "Interior is disconnected",
    "Nested shells",
    "Duplicate Rings",
    "Too few points",
    "Invalid Coordinate",
    "Repeated Point",
    "Ring is not closed",
]

def classify_reason(message):
    for category in GEOS_CATEGORIES:
        if message.startswith(category):
            return category
    return "Other"

def diagnose(geom):
    if geom.is_valid:
        return True, "", ""
    message = explain_validity(geom)
    m = POSITION_RE.match(message)
    reason = m.group(1).strip() if m else message
    position = f"{m.group(2)} {m.group(3)}" if m else ""
    return False, classify_reason(reason), position

diagnosis = gdf.geometry.apply(diagnose)
gdf["valid"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[0])
gdf["category"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[1])
gdf["position"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[2])

# Keep every original column from the uploaded file, not just "name":
# a missing value (None) in one of them would otherwise vanish
# silently once this result is serialized to JSON for the browser,
# instead of showing up as an empty value.
for col in gdf.columns:
    if col != "geometry":
        gdf[col] = gdf[col].fillna("")

{"features": gdf.__geo_interface__, "originalCrsFeatures": export_crs(gdf).__geo_interface__, "crsWarning": crs_warning}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #geometry-diagnose-r}
#| package: sf, geojsonsf, jsonlite
library(sf)
library(geojsonsf)
data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}
if (is.null(data)) {
  wkt <- "POLYGON((12.45 41.85, 12.55 41.95, 12.45 41.95, 12.55 41.85, 12.45 41.85))"
  data <- st_sf(name = "bowtie", geometry = st_as_sfc(wkt, crs = 4326))
}

# Diagnosis and the map both need WGS84 (GeoJSON/MapLibre assume it) —
# original_crs/export_crs stay in the session as globals, reused by
# geometry-repair-r below to reproject BACK before a download.
crs_warning <- NULL
original_crs <- st_crs(data)
if (is.na(original_crs)) {
  st_crs(data) <- 4326
  original_crs <- st_crs(data)
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
} else if (!isTRUE(original_crs == st_crs(4326))) {
  data <- st_transform(data, 4326)
}

export_crs <- function(d) {
  if (is.null(d) || isTRUE(original_crs == st_crs(4326))) return(d)
  st_transform(d, original_crs)
}

if (!("name" %in% names(data))) {
  data$name <- paste("geometry", seq_len(nrow(data)))
}

data$valid <- st_is_valid(data)
data$reason <- st_is_valid(data, reason = TRUE)
data$reason[data$valid] <- NA

# GEOS reports one of a small, CLOSED set of validity failures --
# verified against TopologyValidationError.cpp in the GEOS source
# itself (see "Gallery of geometric errors" below). st_is_valid(reason
# = TRUE) uses those SAME exact strings when GEOS is the engine
# actually running (sf_use_s2(FALSE)) -- but not with S2, sf's own
# DEFAULT for geographic coordinates like this article's examples:
# S2 reports WHICH edges cross, not WHICH of GEOS's named categories
# the crossing represents, because its own validity model has no such
# categories (see "Valid according to whom?" above). Classified only
# when GEOS is actually in use; labeled "S2 (no GEOS category)"
# otherwise, with the raw S2 message still shown in "reason" -- forcing
# it into a GEOS category it was never reported against would be a
# guess, not a classification.
GEOS_CATEGORIES <- c(
  "Ring Self-intersection",
  "Self-intersection",
  "Hole lies outside shell",
  "Holes are nested",
  "Interior is disconnected",
  "Nested shells",
  "Duplicate Rings",
  "Too few points",
  "Invalid Coordinate",
  "Repeated Point",
  "Ring is not closed"
)
classify_reason <- function(message, uses_s2) {
  if (is.na(message)) return(NA_character_)
  if (uses_s2) return("S2 (no GEOS category)")
  for (category in GEOS_CATEGORIES) {
    if (startsWith(message, category)) return(category)
  }
  "Other"
}
uses_s2 <- sf_use_s2()
data$category <- vapply(data$reason, classify_reason, character(1), uses_s2 = uses_s2)

list(
  features = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(data), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  originalCrsFeatures = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(export_crs(data)), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  crsWarning = crs_warning
)
```

:::

## Same spatial question, two languages

Python and R answer the same question with one line each:

**Python**

```python
gdf.geometry.is_valid
```

**R**

```r
sf::st_is_valid(data)
```

Both go through the same geometry engine, GEOS, for this calculation.[^reason-text]

[^reason-text]: Don't expect the exact same text when you ask *why* a
geometry is invalid, though: `explain_validity()` in Python includes
the coordinates of the problem (e.g. `"Self-intersection[12.5
41.9]"`), while `st_is_valid(reason = TRUE)` in R describes the edges
involved without coordinates (e.g. `"Edge 0 crosses edge 2"`): same
calculation, different vocabulary. Not a bug in either one, just a
detail that distinguishes one spatial ecosystem from the other.

## Valid according to whom?

"Valid" isn't absolute: it depends on the geometric model and the
engine checking it.

- **Python** → `shapely` → always GEOS.
- **R** → `sf` → GEOS or S2, depending on `sf::sf_use_s2()`.

For the diagnosis above the difference doesn't show. It becomes
concrete in the repair, below:

::: {.callout-important}
**Why `sf_use_s2(FALSE)` before `st_make_valid()`?** With geographic
coordinates (lon/lat) and `sf_use_s2(TRUE)` (the default),
`st_make_valid()` in R dispatches to `s2::s2_rebuild()` instead of
GEOS: a different algorithm that, on these cases, **fixes nothing**,
returning the geometry unchanged without an error. Verified not just
on webR but also on real R 4.3.3 with sf 1.0.15: this isn't a bug in
this project, it's documented `sf` behavior (see issues #1985 and
#1771 on [r-spatial/sf](https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/1985)).
Forcing `sf_use_s2(FALSE)` routes the call through GEOS, which works
correctly here; it's turned back on right after, because other
operations (distances, areas) on geographic coordinates benefit from
S2. `shapely` in Python doesn't have this problem because it has no
alternative S2 engine: it always goes through GEOS.
:::

## Gallery of geometric errors

GEOS reports one of a small, closed set of validity failures, not a
free-text description: an exact list, verified against
[TopologyValidationError.cpp](https://github.com/libgeos/geos/blob/main/src/operation/valid/TopologyValidationError.cpp)
in the GEOS source itself. The diagnose cells above match every
message to one of these names, shown in the "category" column; a
message that matches none of them shows up as "Other" rather than
being forced into the closest one.

::: {.table-responsive}

| Category | What happens | Example below |
|---|---|:-:|
| Self-intersection | The boundary crosses itself | ✓ |
| Ring Self-intersection | The boundary touches itself at a point, without crossing | ✓ |
| Hole lies outside shell | A hole sits entirely outside the outer boundary\* | ✓ |
| Holes are nested | A hole contains its own shell\* | ✓ |
| Interior is disconnected | A hole splits the interior into pieces that don't connect | — |
| Nested shells | One polygon's shell sits entirely inside another's, in a `MultiPolygon` | — |
| Too few points | A ring has fewer than the 4 points a closed ring needs | — |
| Invalid Coordinate | A coordinate is `NaN` or infinite | — |
| Repeated Point | The same point twice in a row | — |
| Duplicate Rings | Two rings describe the exact same boundary | — |
| Ring is not closed | A ring's first and last point don't match | — |

:::

\* Valid under R's default S2 engine, invalid under GEOS: see [Where
R and Python actually
disagree](#where-r-and-python-actually-disagree), past Repair.

Of the rows without an example, "Interior is disconnected" belongs to
the same family as the crossing cases below, "Nested shells" needs two
full polygons to set up, and "Too few points" and "Invalid Coordinate"
are rarely produced by a real file. The last three are worth being
honest about: they're real GEOS categories the classifier still
recognizes if they ever show up, but none of them could be reproduced
through an actual upload here. As of GEOS 3.11+, a repeated point is
reported as "Too few points" instead (verified live, not assumed from
the changelog). Every duplicate-ring construction tried got caught as
"Self-intersection" first, before that check ever ran. And both
GeoJSON and Shapefile close every ring at the file format level,
before geopandas or sf ever see it, so an unclosed ring never reaches
GEOS.

Each example below loads its own data into the diagnosis cell pair
above. No repair here, that's in the Repair section further down.

### Self-intersection ("bowtie")

<svg viewBox="0 0 220 200" style="max-width: 240px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" role="img" aria-label="Bowtie polygon: the boundary crosses itself at the center, without any special vertex there">
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="218" height="198" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#5a4f3e" stroke-width="1"/>
  <path d="M 20 140 L 200 20 L 20 20 L 200 140 Z" fill="#e05252" fill-opacity="0.35" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="110" y="176" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="12" fill="#2a2117">self-intersection</text>
</svg>

The polygon's boundary crosses itself, forming a bowtie shape instead
of a single closed area. It's the most common case in practice, often
the result of imprecise manual digitizing.

::: {.webgeods-example py="geometry-diagnose-py" r="geometry-diagnose-r" label="📋 Load this example"}

# that represents, since its own validity model has no such names.
GEOS_CATEGORIES <- c(
  "Ring Self-intersection",

### A hole that crosses the boundary

<svg viewBox="0 0 260 250" style="max-width: 240px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" role="img" aria-label="Polygon with a hole extending outside the outer boundary">
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="258" height="248" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#5a4f3e" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="40" y="40" width="160" height="160" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <rect x="140" y="40" width="60" height="80" fill="#f3ede1"/>
  <rect x="140" y="20" width="100" height="20" fill="#e05252" fill-opacity="0.7"/>
  <rect x="200" y="40" width="40" height="80" fill="#e05252" fill-opacity="0.7"/>
  <rect x="140" y="20" width="100" height="100" fill="none" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
  <text x="130" y="228" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#2a2117">hole extends past the boundary</text>
</svg>

A "hole" (inner ring, e.g. a lake inside a land polygon) must lie
entirely within the outer boundary. Here it doesn't: one corner sticks
out past the shell's own edge.

::: {.callout-note}
**This is "Self-intersection", not "Hole lies outside shell".** Load
the example and check the category column: GEOS classifies it as a
self-intersection, because the hole's ring literally *crosses* the
shell's ring at that corner: a crossing is a crossing, whichever ring
it happens between. GEOS's own "Hole lies outside shell" category
needs the hole to be entirely disjoint from the shell, with no
crossing at all. That's the next example.
:::

::: {.webgeods-example py="geometry-diagnose-py" r="geometry-diagnose-r" label="📋 Load this example"}
```python
import re
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import shape
from shapely.validation import explain_validity

geom = shape({
  "type": "Polygon",
  "coordinates": [
    [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 4], [0, 4], [0, 0]],
    [[3, 3], [5, 3], [5, 5], [3, 5], [3, 3]]
  ]
})
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": ["hole-outside-boundary"]}, geometry=[geom], crs="EPSG:4326")

# Same session-globals contract as the diagnose cell above (gdf/
# original_crs/export_crs stay in the session, reused by Repair
# further down) — this example is already WGS84, so export_crs() is a
# no-op passthrough here, kept for the contract rather than because
# this particular shape needs reprojecting.
crs_warning = None
original_crs = gdf.crs

def export_crs(g):
    if g is None or original_crs is None or original_crs == "EPSG:4326":
        return g
    return g.to_crs(original_crs)

# Same diagnose() as the main diagnose cell above.
POSITION_RE = re.compile(r"^(.*?)\[([-\d.]+)\s+([-\d.]+)\]$")

GEOS_CATEGORIES = [
    "Ring Self-intersection",
    "Self-intersection",
    "Hole lies outside shell",
    "Holes are nested",
    "Interior is disconnected",
    "Nested shells",
    "Duplicate Rings",
    "Too few points",
    "Invalid Coordinate",
    "Repeated Point",
    "Ring is not closed",
]

def classify_reason(message):
    for category in GEOS_CATEGORIES:
        if message.startswith(category):
            return category
    return "Other"

def diagnose(geom):
    if geom.is_valid:
        return True, "", ""
    message = explain_validity(geom)
    m = POSITION_RE.match(message)
    reason = m.group(1).strip() if m else message
    position = f"{m.group(2)} {m.group(3)}" if m else ""
    return False, classify_reason(reason), position

diagnosis = gdf.geometry.apply(diagnose)
gdf["valid"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[0])
gdf["category"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[1])
gdf["position"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[2])

{"features": gdf.__geo_interface__, "originalCrsFeatures": export_crs(gdf).__geo_interface__, "crsWarning": crs_warning}
```
```r
library(sf)
library(geojsonsf)
wkt <- "POLYGON((0 0, 4 0, 4 4, 0 4, 0 0), (3 3, 5 3, 5 5, 3 5, 3 3))"
data <- st_sf(name = "hole-outside-boundary", geometry = st_as_sfc(wkt, crs = 4326))

# Same session-globals contract as the diagnose cell above (data/
# original_crs/export_crs stay in the session, reused by Repair
# further down) — this example is already WGS84, so export_crs() is a
# no-op passthrough here, kept for the contract rather than because
# this particular shape needs reprojecting.
crs_warning <- NULL
original_crs <- st_crs(data)

export_crs <- function(d) {
  if (is.null(d) || isTRUE(original_crs == st_crs(4326))) return(d)
  st_transform(d, original_crs)
}

data$valid <- st_is_valid(data)
data$reason <- st_is_valid(data, reason = TRUE)
data$reason[data$valid] <- NA

# Same classify_reason() as the main diagnose cell above -- see its
# own comment for why this is "S2 (no GEOS category)" by
# default: S2 reports which edges cross, not which named GEOS failure
# that represents, since its own validity model has no such names.
GEOS_CATEGORIES <- c(
  "Ring Self-intersection",
  "Self-intersection",
  "Hole lies outside shell",
  "Holes are nested",
  "Interior is disconnected",
  "Nested shells",
  "Duplicate Rings",
  "Too few points",
  "Invalid Coordinate",
  "Repeated Point",
  "Ring is not closed"
)
classify_reason <- function(message, uses_s2) {
  if (is.na(message)) return(NA_character_)
  if (uses_s2) return("S2 (no GEOS category)")
  for (category in GEOS_CATEGORIES) {
    if (startsWith(message, category)) return(category)
  }
  "Other"
}
uses_s2 <- sf_use_s2()
data$category <- vapply(data$reason, classify_reason, character(1), uses_s2 = uses_s2)

list(
  features = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(data), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  originalCrsFeatures = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(export_crs(data)), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  crsWarning = crs_warning
)
```
:::

### A hole with no crossing at all

<svg viewBox="0 0 260 200" style="max-width: 240px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" role="img" aria-label="Polygon with a hole positioned entirely outside the outer boundary, not touching it">
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="258" height="198" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#5a4f3e" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="30" y="30" width="120" height="140" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <rect x="190" y="60" width="50" height="50" fill="none" stroke="#e05252" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
  <text x="140" y="188" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#2a2117">hole sits entirely outside the shell</text>
</svg>

Same rule as above (a hole must lie entirely within the shell), but
this time nothing crosses: the "hole" ring sits well clear of the
shell's own boundary, disjoint from it. This is what GEOS's own "Hole
lies outside shell" category actually needs. A hole that merely
*crosses* the boundary (previous example) is a self-intersection
instead, a different failure with a different name.

Load this example and run it in both languages: R's "valid" column
shows ✓ where Python's shows ✗. That's not a quirk of this one case; see
[Where R and Python actually
disagree](#where-r-and-python-actually-disagree) near the end of the
page for why.

::: {.webgeods-example py="geometry-diagnose-py" r="geometry-diagnose-r" label="📋 Load this example"}
```python
import re
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import shape
from shapely.validation import explain_validity

geom = shape({
  "type": "Polygon",
  "coordinates": [
    [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 4], [0, 4], [0, 0]],
    [[6, 2], [7, 2], [7, 3], [6, 3], [6, 2]]
  ]
})
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": ["hole-lies-outside-shell"]}, geometry=[geom], crs="EPSG:4326")

# Same session-globals contract as the diagnose cell above.
crs_warning = None
original_crs = gdf.crs

def export_crs(g):
    if g is None or original_crs is None or original_crs == "EPSG:4326":
        return g
    return g.to_crs(original_crs)

# Same diagnose() as the main diagnose cell above.
POSITION_RE = re.compile(r"^(.*?)\[([-\d.]+)\s+([-\d.]+)\]$")

GEOS_CATEGORIES = [
    "Ring Self-intersection",
    "Self-intersection",
    "Hole lies outside shell",
    "Holes are nested",
    "Interior is disconnected",
    "Nested shells",
    "Duplicate Rings",
    "Too few points",
    "Invalid Coordinate",
    "Repeated Point",
    "Ring is not closed",
]

def classify_reason(message):
    for category in GEOS_CATEGORIES:
        if message.startswith(category):
            return category
    return "Other"

def diagnose(geom):
    if geom.is_valid:
        return True, "", ""
    message = explain_validity(geom)
    m = POSITION_RE.match(message)
    reason = m.group(1).strip() if m else message
    position = f"{m.group(2)} {m.group(3)}" if m else ""
    return False, classify_reason(reason), position

diagnosis = gdf.geometry.apply(diagnose)
gdf["valid"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[0])
gdf["category"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[1])
gdf["position"] = diagnosis.apply(lambda t: t[2])

{"features": gdf.__geo_interface__, "originalCrsFeatures": export_crs(gdf).__geo_interface__, "crsWarning": crs_warning}
```

### Ring touching itself (hourglass)

<svg viewBox="0 0 220 250" style="max-width: 240px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" role="img" aria-label="Two lobes of a polygon touching at a single vertex, without crossing">
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="218" height="248" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#5a4f3e" stroke-width="1"/>
  <path d="M 20 20 L 200 20 L 110 110 Z" fill="#e05252" fill-opacity="0.35" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <path d="M 110 110 L 20 200 L 200 200 Z" fill="#e05252" fill-opacity="0.35" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="110" cy="110" r="5" fill="#e05252" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="110" y="228" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="12" fill="#2a2117">a single shared vertex</text>
</svg>

The polygon's boundary touches itself at one point, without crossing,
effectively splitting the shape into two lobes joined by a single
vertex: not cleanly connected, so invalid.

### Overlapping holes

<svg viewBox="0 0 260 290" style="max-width: 240px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" role="img" aria-label="Two holes overlapping inside the same polygon, like a Venn diagram">
  <defs>
    <clipPath id="holeA-clip"><circle cx="105" cy="130" r="55"/></clipPath>
  </defs>
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="258" height="288" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#5a4f3e" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="220" height="220" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.15" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="105" cy="130" r="55" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="155" cy="130" r="55" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="155" cy="130" r="55" fill="#e05252" fill-opacity="0.85" clip-path="url(#holeA-clip)"/>
  <text x="130" y="268" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="12" fill="#2a2117">the two holes overlap</text>
</svg>

If a polygon has more than one hole, they can't overlap each other:
two intersecting holes create an ambiguous area (inside or outside
the polygon?) that the model doesn't allow.

### Holes are nested

<svg viewBox="0 0 220 220" style="max-width: 220px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 1.5rem auto;" role="img" aria-label="A polygon with a hole, and inside that hole a smaller filled island">
  <rect x="1" y="1" width="218" height="218" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#5a4f3e" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="180" height="180" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <rect x="60" y="60" width="100" height="100" fill="#f3ede1" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
  <rect x="90" y="90" width="40" height="40" fill="#42583c" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2a2117" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="110" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#2a2117">a hole, with an island inside it</text>
</svg>

A hole with a smaller shape sitting inside *that* hole, like an island
in a lake inside a larger landmass. The Simple Features model doesn't
allow this as one `Polygon`: a hole containing its own shell is
supposed to be two separate `Polygon`s (the landmass-with-lake, and
the island) combined into a `MultiPolygon`, not nested rings in one.

Load the example and run it in both languages: Python marks it ✗ with
category "Holes are nested". R's default marks it ✓, valid, so it has
no category at all. That's not a wording difference; see [Where R and
Python actually
disagree](#where-r-and-python-actually-disagree) near the end of the
page for why, and why it's not shown in the Repair section below (there's
nothing to repair under R's default, since it isn't flagged invalid
there to begin with).

## Repair (optional)

The diagnosis tells you what's wrong. Repair changes the data:
`make_valid()`/`st_make_valid()` rebuild the geometry into an
equivalent, valid form. **Requires having run the diagnosis above at
least once**: it reuses exactly the same data just diagnosed (`gdf` in
Python, `data` in R stay in the session between one cell and the next,
like in a notebook), with no new reading of the file.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #geometry-repair-py}
#| inject: pyWasReset
if pyWasReset:
    raise RuntimeError("The map was reset since the last diagnosis — run Diagnose (Python) again before Repair.")

from shapely.validation import make_valid

gdf["valid_before"] = gdf["valid"]
gdf["geometry"] = gdf.geometry.apply(lambda g: make_valid(g) if not g.is_valid else g)
gdf["valid_after"] = gdf.geometry.is_valid

# Same reasoning as the diagnose cell above: keep every original
# column, fillna("") so a None doesn't silently drop that property.
for col in gdf.columns:
    if col != "geometry":
        gdf[col] = gdf[col].fillna("")

{"features": gdf.__geo_interface__, "originalCrsFeatures": export_crs(gdf).__geo_interface__}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #geometry-repair-r}
#| inject: rWasReset
if (isTRUE(rWasReset)) {
  stop("The map was reset since the last diagnosis -- run Diagnose (R) again before Repair.")
}

library(sf)
library(geojsonsf)
data$valid_before <- data$valid

# With geographic coordinates, sf routes st_make_valid() through S2
# by default -- a different algorithm from GEOS that, on some of
# these exact cases, fixes nothing and returns the geometry unchanged
# without an error. Forcing GEOS here (sf_use_s2(FALSE)) is what
# actually repairs them; turned back on right after, since other
# operations (distances, areas) benefit from S2 on geographic data.
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
data <- st_make_valid(data)
sf_use_s2(TRUE)

data$valid_after <- st_is_valid(data)

list(
  features = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(data), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  originalCrsFeatures = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(export_crs(data)), simplifyVector = FALSE)
)
```

:::

The table and the report above update themselves: the
`valid_before`/`valid_after` columns automatically appear next to the
diagnosis ones.

## Where R and Python actually disagree {#where-r-and-python-actually-disagree}

Two examples in the gallery above ("A hole with no crossing at all"
and "Holes are nested") show R's default marking valid (✓) a geometry
Python marks invalid (✗). Not a wording difference like the rest of the
gallery: a genuine disagreement on whether the geometry is even
invalid, worth its own explanation instead of a quick aside inside
those two sections.

**Neither engine is wrong.** `S2Polygon`'s own validity rule for a set
of loops is just "no pair of loops that cross"; a hole that doesn't
touch the shell trivially satisfies that, whatever else it is. GEOS
enforces the stricter OGC Simple Features rule instead: a `Polygon`'s
hole is supposed to describe a piece cut out of its shell, so one that
doesn't touch the shell at all can't be describing that, crossing or
not. Same story with nested holes: `S2Polygon`'s own model builds a
polygon's interior from an odd/even rule over nested loop
*depth*: shells at depth 0, holes at depth 1, and a **shell at depth
2** is just as legitimate a structure as depth 0, not a
violation.[^s2polygon-depth] GEOS's OGC rule says a single `Polygon`
may have a shell and holes, full stop; a shell-within-a-hole has to be
a separate `Polygon`, combined into a `MultiPolygon` instead. Two
different definitions of "valid polygon," not one calculation read
two ways.

`sf_use_s2(FALSE)` (see "Valid according to whom?" above) makes R's
answer match Python's in both cases.

[^s2polygon-depth]: From Google's own S2 documentation: "the given
loops are automatically converted into a canonical form consisting of
'shells' and 'holes' ... nested hierarchically. 'Outer shell' loops
have depth 0, holes within those loops have depth 1, shells within
those holes have depth 2, etc." (see
[s2geometry.io/devguide/basic_types](http://s2geometry.io/devguide/basic_types.html)).
Verified live against the nested-holes example, not just read off the
docs: reversing every ring's winding order in all four combinations
still leaves R's default S2 check reporting "Valid Geometry", so it
isn't a ring-orientation artifact either; it's the nesting itself
that S2 accepts and GEOS doesn't.

Neither case is shown in the Repair section above: there's nothing to
repair under R's default (neither is flagged invalid there to begin
with), and Python's own `make_valid()` would just restructure them
into a `MultiPolygon`/simplified shape the same way it already does
for the other examples. What matters here is the disagreement itself,
not the fix.

## What about relationships between geometries?

A geometry can be perfectly valid on its own and still be wrong in
relation to other geometries: two valid polygons overlapping when
they shouldn't, a gap between areas that should touch. That's a
different problem: topology. It's covered in
[Topology Errors in a GeoJSON](topology-errors.qmd).
